question_en:
I plan to visit the protected area where the species in the image is located during the same month the photo was taken to observe butterflies, and to learn about other butterflies there that belong to the same family and have similar appearances. Please answer the following three parts in order:

(1) What species is the butterfly in the attachment, and what is the protected area where it is located? Please find the official 2024 butterfly checklist for this protected area and list all confirmed members of the same family in the checklist as the candidate range for subsequent filtering.

(2) Among the candidates identified in part (1), which butterflies have, on each forewing, a continuous light-colored area covering more than half of the wing and at least three separate dark bands that taper inward from the long edge nearest the head without reaching the opposite edge?

(3) Among the species filtered in part (2), which species have an adult activity season covering August, and whose state-level status is neither SX nor SH? Please provide the names of the species that finally meet the criteria.

Answer format: For part 1, first provide the species, protected area, and the link to the 2024 checklist in text, then use a table to list the names and scientific names of all members of the same family; for parts 2 and 3, list the species matching the appearance and the final species names respectively in text.
answer:
Part 1: Species: Eastern Tiger Swallowtail (Papilio glaucus); Protected Area: Shenandoah National Park.
2024 Official Butterfly Checklist: https://www.nps.gov/shen/learn/nature/upload/508_SHEN_SpeciesChecklist_Butterflies.pdf

| Species Name | Scientific Name |
| --- | --- |
| Pipevine Swallowtail | Battus philenor |
| Zebra Swallowtail | Eurytides marcellus |
| Appalachian Tiger Swallowtail | Papilio appalachiensis |
| Giant Swallowtail | Papilio cresphontes |
| Eastern Tiger Swallowtail | Papilio glaucus |
| Palamedes Swallowtail | Papilio palamedes |
| Black Swallowtail | Papilio polyxenes |
| Spicebush Swallowtail | Papilio troilus |

Part 2: Appalachian Tiger Swallowtail; Eastern Tiger Swallowtail.

Part 3: Eastern Tiger Swallowtail (Papilio glaucus).

# Detailed Simulated Search Trajectory · 8-1-D02-2

## Step 01 · Locate original park photo from input butterfly image

Action: Search for "Eastern Tiger Swallowtail park photo" using light yellow wing surface, tiger stripes, and tail streamers, and verify against the NPS gallery.

Evidence Observation: The input corresponds to the official photo of Eastern Tiger Swallowtail (Papilio glaucus), located in Shenandoah National Park. The ImageCreateDate for the identically named image in the original gallery is 2013-07-26, while the task package seed_provenance records 2013-08-16; there is a conflict in the date materials. Do not present either date as a confirmed date when the photo was taken. Subsequent season questions are handled according to August, as explicitly specified in part 3.

Evidence Link:
https://www.nps.gov/media/photo/gallery.htm?id=7D5B7DEE-1DD8-B71B-0B7B7879C0507D86

Result of this step: Identified species and park, and proceeded to the 2024 official checklist.

## Step 02 · Extract complete rows for the same family from the official 2024 checklist

Action: Obtain the park's PDF, verify the version and the Papilionidae family section; simultaneously read the season legend and the state-level status column.

Evidence Observation: There are 8 candidates; Zebra Swallowtail is also listed in the checklist, so the earlier list of seven species that omitted it cannot be used.

| Eastern Tiger Swallowtail | Papilio glaucus |
| Palamedes Swallowtail | Papilio palamedes |

| Spicebush Swallowtail | Papilio troilus |

Evidence Link:

Result of this step: Fixed 8 members of the same family, retaining the complete range.

## Step 03 · Prepare unified dorsal spread comparison images

Action: For each species, look up dorsal images of adult butterflies with wings spread, confirm that most of both forewings are visible, and use retained files corresponding to their sources.

Evidence Observation: Conditions are judged per forewing: a continuous light-colored area covering more than half, and at least three separate dark bands that taper inward from the long edge nearest the head without reaching the opposite edge. Scattered light spots or light bands on a dark background do not substitute for a continuous light background.

Evidence Link:
https://www.nps.gov/shen/learn/nature/upload/508_SHEN_SpeciesChecklist_Butterflies.pdf

Result of this step: Check all 8 species one by one, first making appearance judgments, then checking seasons.

## Step 04 · Check species one by one: Pipevine Swallowtail

Action: Open the source image and examine the continuous background color area and the direction, spacing, and termination position of dark bands along the left and right forewings separately.

Evidence Observation: The forewing has a dark blue-black background, failing the requirement for a continuous light-colored area covering more than half; there are no qualified tapering dark bands on a light background.

Evidence Link:
https://commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/File:Battus_philenor_-_dorsal.jpg
https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/4/41/Battus_philenor_-_dorsal.jpg

## Step 05 · Check species one by one: Zebra Swallowtail

Action: Open the source image and examine the continuous background color area and the direction, spacing, and termination position of dark bands along the left and right forewings separately.

Evidence Observation: In UF/IFAS Image 1, black dominates the forewing, with light colors appearing as separate bands; the dark bands traverse the wing surface, rather than being at least three isolated finger-like bands tapering inward on a large continuous light background. This is UF/IFAS Image 1, adopted on 2026-09-28 to fill the official omission of this member; the source's open license status is unconfirmed, so it should not be described as a Commons openly licensed image.

Evidence Observation: Each visible forewing has a light-colored area covering more than half, with 4 separate dark bands tapering inward from the long edge nearest the head.

Action: For Appalachian Tiger and Eastern Tiger, check the corresponding rows in the same PDF version, map August to "summer" according to the PDF legend; additionally consult the NatureServe explanation for state-level codes.

Evidence Observation: In the PDF legend, "summer" corresponds to June–August. SX denotes presumed extinct within the state/region, and SH denotes possibly extinct; this question examines state-level S codes and does not substitute global G codes for state-level judgments.

https://www.nps.gov/shen/learn/nature/upload/508_SHEN_SpeciesChecklist_Butterflies.pdf
